sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No.
   - **Where:** the headline "The river ferry through the seasons" (about x 120–742, y 68–104) sits over three columns.
   - **What the viewer meets:** the headline promises an account of how the ferry changes over the year. The body doesn't give one. Column 1 (x 120–380) covers the route, how often boats run and how long a crossing takes. Column 2 (x 436–696) covers bicycles on board. Only column 3 (x 752–1012) is about a season, the winter timetable. A reader looking for the seasonal story finds it in one paragraph out of three. A reader who wants the times or the bicycle rules gets no sign of them from the headline, and the columns have no subheads to help them scan.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6 says headings describe the topic of their section. The catalog notes this line rests on reading the content, so here it is partly a judgment of the copy.
   - **Fix:** make the headline name what the page actually holds, such as the timetable, bicycles and winter changes. Or, if the seasonal angle is the point, make the body deliver it (summer against winter service, tides and weather). If the three columns stay as separate topics, a short label over each would let a reader go straight to the one they need.
   - **Type and weight:** convention. Minor: the page still reads as ferry information, but the headline steers the reader slightly wrong and scanning is slower.

**What's working.**
- **Nothing extra:** there are no rules, boxes or ornament. A heading and three text blocks, which is all a short service-information page needs.
- **Clean pairing:** the bold sans headline over the serif body is a familiar pairing, and the type and colours feel like one piece. The near-black on white feels calm, which suits practical service information.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each heading names what its section holds)

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The title, "The river ferry through the seasons" (about x 120–742, y 68–104), is clearly the first thing you see. It is a bold, dark sans serif at about twice the body size, so the eye knows where to start without help.
- The title differs from the body in more than size. It is a bold sans serif, and the three body columns (x 120–1012, y 145–510) are a regular serif. The difference in weight and letterform makes the two levels separate at a glance, which size alone would not.

Outside the checklist, for the director: the piece has only two levels, the title and the body. Each column covers a different topic (the timetable and crossings, bicycles, winter and notices), and none has a subhead. To find a topic, a reader has to read the column. A small subhead on each column would fix this. This is taste, not a checklist failure. Also, the title promises "through the seasons", but only the third column is about a season.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No.
   - **Where:** The headline and all three columns sit in the top-left part of the frame, from about x 120 to 1012 and y 65 to 510. The margins don't match: about 120 px on the left, about 268 px on the right, and about 290 px of empty space below the longest column.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The page looks pulled up and to the left. The empty strip on the right is almost as wide as a fourth column, so it reads as space the layout forgot to fill, as if the piece was built for a wider page and dropped into this one. It doesn't look like a chosen asymmetric margin, because nothing on the right or bottom balances the weight of the text.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight, and a lopsided layout with no visible intent is a fault.
   - **Fix:** Either make the asymmetry look intended or remove it. To make it intended, give the empty area a job: a wider outer margin used for a picture, a pull quote or a caption. To remove it, centre the three-column block in the frame, or widen the columns until the right margin matches the left. A layout that adjusts to the frame width would solve it at any size.
   - **Kind:** Convention.
   - **Weight:** Minor. The text still reads in order. This changes how finished the page looks, not whether it does its job.

**What's working.**
- **The grid is strict.** The three columns are the same width (about 260 px) with equal gutters (about 56 px), and the headline lines up with the first column's left edge at x 120. The page reads as one system, not as blocks placed one at a time.
- **Lines line up across columns.** Lines of text sit on the same baselines in all three columns (about y 154, 181, 207 and down), so the rows read as even horizontal bands. This is why the uneven column endings (about y 500, 447 and 473) look calm rather than messy.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances).

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does justified text keep even word spaces, with no holes or rivers of white?** It doesn't. All three columns (x ≈ 120–380, 436–696, 752–1012, y ≈ 145–510) are justified with no hyphenation, so many lines are stretched until there are holes between the words:
   - Column 1: "minutes between early" (y ≈ 234), "weather, and a little" (y ≈ 340), "longer when the tide" (y ≈ 367), "sandbank near the old" (y ≈ 473).
   - Column 2: "Riders wheel them on" (y ≈ 207), "bicycle during the" (y ≈ 367), where each gap is wider than a whole word, and "stays clear for people" (y ≈ 420).
   - Column 3: "In winter the timetable" (y ≈ 154), "dusk. Printed timetables" and "each landing, and the" (y ≈ 260–314).

   On the stacked loose lines in column 1 (y ≈ 340–367) and column 2 (y ≈ 340–367), the gaps line up into white channels running down the column. The gaps are the first thing you notice in the text. The grey of each column breaks into spots, the eye jumps across each hole, and reading turns jerky. The cause is justifying a measure this short: Bringhurst (*Elements*, 2.1.1–2.1.2) warns that short justified lines lead to "white acne", and Hochuli (*Detail in Typography*, p. 34) says that under about 50 characters even word spacing "becomes difficult, if not impossible". Fix: set the columns flush left, ragged right. Keep justification only if the columns get wider (see 2) and hyphenation is turned on. Defect. **Major.**

2. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** They don't. Each column is about 260 px wide and holds roughly 28–32 characters a line. That is below Bringhurst's 40–50 for text set in several columns (*Elements*, 2.1.2). The reader has to return to a new line every few words, and the short measure is the direct cause of finding 1. The page has room for wider columns: about 270 px are empty to the right of column 3 (x ≈ 1012–1280). Fix: widen the columns into the empty space toward 40–50 characters, or use two columns instead of three. Convention (Bringhurst), and here it costs the reader something. **Major.**

**What's working.**
- The pairing works: a bold sans headline over a serif made for reading, two clearly different faces with clear jobs and nothing close enough to clash. The body is a comfortable size, about 19 px, near-black on white.
- The headline is one line with tidy spacing (checked in a crop), and the columns keep a crisp left edge. The last lines ("harbour wall.", "high tide.") are two-word endings, not single-word runts.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; even word spacing in justified text)

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the bold dark headline at top left, then drops into three justified serif columns. It reads as a plain editorial article page about a river ferry, calm and quiet. The right third and the bottom third of the page are empty white.

Job (assumed): an informational web article or page for ferry passengers.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. It uses only near-black text, a slightly cooler dark gray in the headline, and white.
- Saturated color kept small: yes. There is no saturated color.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text sits on white, and the structure holds in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There are no hues, so nothing to get wrong.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The body text is the same tone in all three columns.
- Neighboring strong colors differ in lightness: yes. There are no neighboring strong colors.
- Status colors used for their meaning: yes. There are none.
- Color-only meaning: yes. Nothing is coded by color.
- Dark theme gray, not black: yes. It is not a dark theme.

No line was answered no or unsure, so there are no entries to open.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** Dark text on white gives the most contrast a reading page can have (the headline at about 120,70–745,105 and the body columns at about 120–1012, 145–510), so the three columns read easily and the structure survives grayscale unchanged. Leaving out accent color is right for a quiet informational article: nothing pulls the eye away from the text. Color is not where this page's problems are; any problems are in the type and the layout.
